We examine a beeping network where nodes communicate via brief radio signals, known as beeps, and operate under strict energy constraints. Our primary objective is to minimize energy usage by ensuring that nodes spend the majority of their time in sleep mode. We introduce a randomized algorithm that enables a node to detect beeps from a specific target with high probability while maintaining low energy consumption. This approach is applicable to any network topology, provided the node possesses knowledge of its own degree and the total number of nodes. Our method achieves a competitive ratio of $O(\log^2 n)$, where $n$ represents the network size. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(\log^2 n)$ for the competitive ratio of any algorithm that guarantees beep detection with high probability. This result demonstrates that our algorithm is asymptotically optimal. Additionally, we explore the application of this algorithm in distributed systems, specifically for enabling nodes to listen to a designated target. We prove that, in the worst-case scenario, a node must listen to the target for at least $\Omega(\log n)$ rounds to ensure detection with high probability. Consequently, our algorithm is also optimal in this context. Finally, we extend our approach to scenarios where nodes lack knowledge of the network size, showing that the algorithm remains effective in such settings. Our findings are supported by experimental results. The paper also includes a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance. This study employs first-principles calculations to analyze the pressure-dependent isotope effect on the critical temperature ($T_c$) of H$_3$S hydride superconductors. By utilizing the Eliashberg theory of strong-coupling superconductivity, we compute the isotope coefficient $\alpha$ across a range of pressures. Our results indicate that $\alpha$ varies with pressure, reaching a maximum of 0.50 at 150 GPa and decreasing to 0.30 at 200 GPa. Furthermore, we observe that $\alpha$ exhibits a sharp decline near the van Hove singularity (VHS) pressure of 170 GPa. This behavior is attributed to the suppression of the electron-phonon coupling constant $\lambda$ as the pressure approaches the VHS. Additionally, we find that the isotope effect on $T_c$ diminishes as pressure increases. These findings offer valuable insights for future experimental investigations. Finally, our calculated $T_c$ values align well with existing experimental data. The source code for the calculations is accessible at https://github.com/abhisheksingh1997/epc. Visual relocalization is a critical component of many robotic applications, including 3D mapping, SLAM, and autonomous driving. This paper introduces a new method that combines hand-crafted features with deep learning to achieve accurate and robust relocalization. Our approach utilizes a 3D surfel map to generate a set of candidate poses for each image. To enhance the discriminative power of these candidates, we employ deep learning to extract features from the map, which are then fused with image features. This integration allows our method to achieve high accuracy even under challenging conditions, such as limited visual features, repetitive structures, and significant viewpoint changes. Experimental results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques across multiple benchmark datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/DFSM. Furthermore, the method is available as a plugin for the open-source SLAM framework ORB-SLAM3. The corresponding paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.07029. We welcome any feedback. This study addresses the challenge of selecting a collaborative user group and designing their precoders within a multiuser MIMO framework. The objective is to minimize total transmit power while ensuring that the sum of the mean square errors (MSE) for all users remains below a specified threshold. To achieve this, we formulate a non-convex optimization problem. By applying a change of variables and introducing an auxiliary variable, we transform the original formulation into an equivalent convex one. We then develop an efficient algorithm to solve this convex problem, demonstrating its convergence to the optimal solution. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between the solutions of the equivalent convex problem and the original non-convex problem. Finally, numerical simulations are provided to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm significantly reduces transmit power compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, it exhibits superior performance in terms of both power consumption and MSE relative to other collaborative user selection and precoding techniques. Finally, the algorithm demonstrates robustness against channel estimation errors. These findings suggest that the proposed method is highly suitable for practical applications. We demonstrate that logical function semifields associated with tropical curves, constructed using the maximum semiring operations on $\mathbb{R}$, are finitely generated as semifields over the tropical semifield $\mathbb{T}$. This finding extends a result by Maclagan and R\"{o}dl, who proved that rational tropical functions on tropical linear spaces are finitely produced over $\mathbb{T}$. Furthermore, our proof yields an effective upper bound for the number of generators. As a consequence, we establish that the semiring of tropical piecewise linear functions on a tropical linear space is finitely generated over $\mathbb{T}$. Additionally, we present a counterexample showing that this finite generation property does not necessarily hold for all tropical varieties. Finally, we provide a counterexample to a conjecture by Maclagan and R\"{o}dl regarding the finite generation of rational tropical functions on tropical varieties. The $Q$-procedure, which is equivalent to the $Q$-learning algorithm, is a widely utilized method for estimating the optimal action-value function. This paper examines the $Q$-procedure within a Markov decision process (MDP) defined by a transition matrix, a reward matrix, and a discount factor. We demonstrate that the procedure consistently converges to the optimal action-value function whenever the product of the discount factor and the second-largest eigenvalue of the transition matrix is strictly less than one. This finding broadens the convergence criteria established by Tsitsiklis and Van Roy (1997) and surpasses the limitations of the stochastic $Q$-learning algorithm. Furthermore, we establish that this convergence condition is both necessary and sufficient for the convergence of the $Q$-procedure to the optimal action-value function. Finally, we illustrate that this result is essential for guaranteeing the convergence of $Q$-learning in continuous-time control problems. Additionally, we present a numerical example to compare the convergence rates of the $Q$-procedure against those reported by Van Roy and Tsitsiklis (1993). The code used to generate the numerical results is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Q-procedure}. The authors gratefully acknowledge Professor Van Roy for his valuable discussions. This paper presents a Vassiliev invariant of order three, denoted as $\mathcal{V}_3$, which is constructed from the Vassiliev invariant of order two, $\mathcal{V}_2$. We demonstrate that $\mathcal{V}_3$ remains invariant under the Fox-Hatcher move. Furthermore, we establish that this move is equivalent to the combination of Reidemeister moves and the twist moves introduced by Kauffman. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the twist move using the invariant $\mathcal{V}_3$. Finally, we calculate the value of $\mathcal{V}_3$ for the trefoil knot. We conducted a theoretical investigation into the potential for nematic instability in LiFeAs, utilizing a model derived from first-principles calculations. By employing the random phase approximation, we determined the spin susceptibility and identified the wave vector that maximizes it. Our results indicate that the susceptibility reaches its peak at the zone center, with no instability occurring at the wave vector associated with the nematic phase. This finding aligns with experimental data, which show that the nematic phase transition in LiFeAs is driven by structural instabilities rather than electronic instabilities. Furthermore, we observed that the susceptibility exhibits a maximum at the zone center across all temperatures, suggesting that LiFeAs does not display a nematic quantum critical point. Additionally, we examined the temperature dependence of the susceptibility and found that it increases as temperature rises, a trend that contradicts the behavior of FeSe. Finally, we analyzed the impact of Li doping on the susceptibility, noting that it diminishes with increasing Li concentration, which is consistent with experimental observations. These results collectively suggest that nematicity in LiFeAs is primarily structural in origin. Our study underscores the critical role of first-principles calculations in elucidating the mechanisms behind nematicity in iron-based superconductors. The methodology employed here can be applied to investigate nematicity in other iron-based superconductors. This study examines the global fit of the two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) in light of recent measurements from the LHC and flavor physics. We analyze the observed 125 GeV Higgs boson properties, the non-observation of a second scalar at the LHC, and constraints derived from flavor-changing neutral current processes. Our results indicate that the 2HDM parameter space is significantly restricted, with the most viable configurations occurring in the Type-I scenario. Furthermore, we explore the potential of the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) and the future Circular e+e- Collider (FCC-ee) to further probe the 2HDM framework. Specifically, we assess the HL-LHC's sensitivity to the lightest CP-even scalar ($h_1$) and the Higgsino mass region, while evaluating the FCC-ee's reach regarding the lightest CP-odd scalar ($a_1$) and the heavy Higgsino sector. Finally, we demonstrate that a comprehensive global fit is essential for accurately constraining the 2HDM parameter space. Our findings suggest that the HL-LHC will substantially narrow down the allowed regions, whereas the FCC-ee will provide complementary constraints on the lightest CP-odd scalar and the heavy Higgsino region. Ultimately, the synergy between these future colliders will enable a thorough investigation of the 2HDM framework. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor R. R. Akhoury. We introduce a novel method for calculating the robust anomaly of chiral gauge theories, which also identifies the theory's stages. This approach is based on the recently developed chiral anomaly inflow mechanism. Our findings align with the established method for determining robust anomalies in chiral gauge theories, which relies on the Dirac index theorem. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the inflow method can identify the theories' stages, a feature that the Dirac index method does not possess. We also examine the robust anomalies of various chiral gauge theories, including those relevant to high-energy physics. Additionally, we explore the relationship between robust anomalies and the robust magnetoelectric effect, which is a hallmark of chiral topological insulators. Finally, we discuss the potential for experimental detection of robust anomalies in chiral gauge theories. This paper examines the initial value problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations within critical Besov spaces. We demonstrate that, unlike the time-dependent case, the steady-state Navier-Stokes equations in these spaces are ill-posed. This finding stands in contrast to the well-posedness of the time-dependent problem in these same spaces. The proof relies on the fact that the linearized steady Navier-Stokes equations admit nontrivial solutions that decay rapidly at infinity. Consequently, we establish that the steady Navier-Stokes equations are ill-posed for initial data of the form $u_0 = u_1 + u_2$, where $u_1$ is a solution to the linearized equations and $u_2$ is an arbitrary function in the critical Besov space. Furthermore, we show that the ill-posedness of the steady Navier-Stokes equations is equivalent to the existence of such solutions to the linearized equations. Finally, we extend this result to the non-homogeneous Navier-Stokes equations. In this context, we prove that the steady equations are ill-posed for initial data $u_0 = u_1 + u_2$, where $u_1$ solves the linearized equations and $u_2$ belongs to a homogeneous Besov space. Additionally, we establish that the ill-posedness of the steady non-homogeneous Navier-Stokes equations is equivalent to the existence of a solution to the linearized equations that decays rapidly at infinity. These findings are derived from a novel characterization of the ill-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces. Specifically, we prove that the Navier-Stokes equations are ill-posed in a critical Besov space if and only if the associated linearized equations possess a solution that decays rapidly at infinity. This characterization is established through the construction of a continuous linear map from the Navier-Stokes equations to the linearized equations. This approach offers an alternative proof of the well-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces, as previously demonstrated by Cannone. Finally, we present an example of a solution to the linearized Navier-Stokes equations that decays rapidly at infinity, thereby confirming the ill-posedness of the steady Navier-Stokes equations in critical Besov spaces. This study examines the nonlinear dynamics of magnons within antiferromagnetic dielectrics. We demonstrate that magnon-magnon interactions generate thermal pressure, which can be modeled as an effective thermal compression of magnons. Furthermore, we show that this thermal compression induces a nonlinear displacement of magnon spectra, shifting them toward lower frequencies. This phenomenon is anticipated to be observable in ultrafast magneto-optical experiments. Additionally, we establish that the nonlinear displacement of magnon spectra arises from the nonlinearity of the magnon dispersion relation. Finally, we illustrate that thermal compression and spectral displacement are universal characteristics of nonlinear waves in antiferromagnetic dielectrics, extending beyond magnons to include other nonlinear excitations such as phonons and magnetoelastic waves. These findings offer a foundation for investigating nonlinear wave phenomena in antiferromagnetic dielectrics. The research was conducted using the first-principles time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) method. We computed the ultrafast dynamics of magnons in yttrium iron garnet (YIG) following a femtosecond laser excitation, revealing that magnon-magnon interactions drive the ultrafast relaxation of the system toward thermal equilibrium. Our results indicate that thermal compression and nonlinear spectral displacement are intrinsic properties of nonlinear waves in antiferromagnetic dielectrics, a conclusion supported by the universality of the governing equations. Loidreau's code-based scheme relies on the existence of a specific linear code $C$ that possesses a dual distance of at least 3, enabling the transformation of a Goppa code $G$ into a structured code $C'$ with a large public kernel. This paper introduces two alternative constructions for the code $C$ that maintain the security of Loidreau's system while offering greater flexibility in selecting the public kernel. The first approach utilizes a concatenated code formed by combining a Reed-Solomon code with a Goppa code, whereas the second approach concatenates a Reed-Solomon code with a shortened Goppa code. Both methods ensure that the resulting public key remains of reasonable size. Furthermore, the code $C$ generated by either method is highly likely to be a Maximum Rank Distance (MRD) code. Finally, the authors demonstrate that Loidreau's original system is a specific instance of the second proposed method. Experimental results indicate that the public key sizes for both proposed systems are comparable to those of Loidreau's initial system. Additionally, the authors present a new attack on the MRD code-based cryptosystem, which serves as a special case of their second proposal. This attack successfully recovers the secret key for small code lengths, thereby highlighting the necessity for larger code lengths in practical applications. The paper concludes with a discussion on the parameters required to achieve a security level of 128 bits. The source code for the attack is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2000/MRDattack}. This study examines the volume of a random simplicial complex generated by a spatial Poisson process, where simplices are included based on the Euclidean distance between their vertices. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of the $k$-dimensional volume as the number of vertices approaches infinity, considering two scenarios: when the inclusion probability is constant and when it varies with the simplex's diameter. Furthermore, we demonstrate the emergence of phase transitions in the homology of random complexes within both scenarios. These transitions are characterized by the minimal spanning $(k+1)$-cycles and the continuity diagrams of the complexes. Finally, we establish the asymptotic properties of these minimal spanning $(k+1)$-cycles and continuity diagrams. The findings are supported by numerical simulations. This work extends the research presented in [1].

Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework designed to train machine learning models across multiple parties holding distinct data. This study investigates the security of VFL within the context of education, where student data is distributed among various institutions. We introduce a novel attack termed "Pragmatic Privacy Assault" (PPA), which leverages the specific characteristics of educational datasets to breach student privacy. Our approach involves constructing a student profile using features from other institutions and utilizing this profile to extract sensitive information from the target institution's data. We demonstrate that PPA successfully infers sensitive attributes such as students' grades and behavioral traits. Furthermore, we show that the effectiveness of PPA is significantly influenced by the volume of data available to the attacker. Finally, we explore potential countermeasures to mitigate the risks posed by PPA in VFL educational environments. Experimental results confirm that our proposed PPA can successfully infer sensitive student attributes, thereby validating the practical threat of privacy leakage in federated learning for education. Additionally, we find that the privacy risk associated with PPA is directly proportional to the amount of data the attacker possesses. To address these challenges, we propose a privacy-preserving strategy for VFL in educational settings that effectively safeguards student privacy. Our evaluation demonstrates that this proposed strategy can substantially reduce the likelihood of privacy leakage caused by PPA. In conclusion, this research underscores the critical importance of privacy protection in VFL for education and offers a viable solution to mitigate associated risks. To address this, we introduce a bag sampling strategy designed to identify and remove noisy labels. This study examines the regularized minimization of the $q$-Rényi distance between two probability distributions, where $q \in (0,1)$, subject to a linear constraint on one of the distributions. We demonstrate that this optimization problem is equivalent to minimizing the Bregman divergence between the distributions, utilizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence as the regularization term. The results indicate that our method outperforms two competing approaches in accuracy, while also exhibiting faster convergence and lower computational costs. Chain event trees (CETs) are widely employed to model the sequential choices individuals make when faced with multiple options. These models are typically estimated using maximum likelihood methods, which yield a single point estimate for the parameters. However, this approach fails to quantify uncertainty regarding the parameters or the resulting predictions. To address this limitation, we introduce a Bayesian framework for estimating chain event networks (CENs), which extend CETs to incorporate prior information. Within this framework, we develop a novel method for selecting the optimal CEN structure by integrating model fit with complexity penalties. This model selection procedure is validated through a simulation study and applied to two real-world datasets: one concerning the factors influencing the choice of a new car, and another examining the factors affecting the choice of a new mobile phone. The results demonstrate that the proposed Bayesian approach effectively balances model fit and complexity while providing a more robust assessment of model uncertainty. Furthermore, the framework facilitates the calculation of Bayesian credible intervals for parameters and predictions, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of uncertainty compared to traditional methods. The code required to replicate this analysis is accessible at https://github.com/robinwagner/chain_event_networks. This paper examines a damped inertial dynamics framework featuring Tikhonov regularization, designed to address ill-posed variational inequalities within Hilbert spaces. The damping term incorporates a logarithmic time decay alongside a vanishing regularization parameter, while the inertial term utilizes a time-decay rate that is slightly faster than $1/t$. Under these conditions, the trajectory converges asymptotically to the minimal norm solution of the variational inequality. Furthermore, the study establishes convergence rates for both the trajectory and its velocity, demonstrating that they decay at identical rates. These findings are supported by numerical experiments. The methodology is applicable to finding the minimal norm fixed point of nonexpansive operators and to identifying the minimal norm element of the solution set for monotone variational inequalities. Additionally, the approach offers a robust alternative to the heavy ball method for solving strongly convex optimization problems. The analysis relies on a Lyapunov function that integrates the Bregman distance, the squared distance to the minimal norm solution, and the Bregman distance of the gradient of the Tikhonov functional. This work extends the research presented in [1].

This study examines how extended contaminants influence the energy-dependent microwave conductivity of kinetic-energy-dominated superconductors. We demonstrate that the conductivity's dependence on the superfluid gap is significantly altered by the presence of extended contaminants, a factor that must be accounted for when analyzing experimental data. Furthermore, we find that the scattering phase of these extended states plays a crucial role in determining the microwave conductivity. Our findings indicate that the scattering phase can be extracted from microwave measurements, offering a potential method to distinguish between various theoretical models of superconductivity. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the cuprate family of superconductors. Our analysis suggests that the extended nature of impurities in cuprates is unlikely to be the primary cause of the observed doping-dependent crossover from Drude to non-Drude behavior in microwave conductivity. Additionally, we show that the scattering phase of extended contaminants can be extracted from cuprate microwave data, yielding a value of approximately 0.5. This result is consistent with the extended nature of impurities in cuprates and supports the kinetic-energy-driven superconductivity model. However, it conflicts with the predictions of the d-wave boson model, which anticipates a scattering phase near 1.0. Consequently, our findings suggest that the boson model may not accurately describe the superconducting state of cuprates. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these results for other unconventional superconductors. Our analysis suggests that the scattering phase of extended contaminants in cuprates is likely similar to that in iron-based superconductors, but differs from the values predicted by the boson model for both material families. The findings indicate that the data aligns with a two-factor model, where the first factor represents a student's aptitude for STEM subjects and the second for those in the social sciences. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be effectively utilized to forecast individual student outcomes. Our results suggest that the model's predictions are highly accurate, with a 90% success rate. Finally, we explore how this model can support educational policy decisions. Specifically, we illustrate its application in identifying students who are either underachieving or overachieving relative to their potential. We show that such students can be pinpointed with 90% accuracy, and we discuss the potential benefits of targeted interventions for these groups. Furthermore, we highlight that the model can detect students who are not performing at their optimal level, offering a pathway to improve their results. We conclude by outlining several avenues for future research. For instance, we propose extending the model to incorporate parental education levels and other relevant factors, which could enable the identification of students who are not receiving adequate support. Additionally, we suggest investigating how the model can be adapted to analyze pathways in other countries and educational systems. Finally, we note that the model can be employed to track changes in student pathways over time, providing valuable insights for policymakers. Our findings indicate that the chiral spin fluid is robust against disorder and can be effectively modeled using Rydberg atoms. Consequently, this state offers a promising avenue for investigating topological phenomena in spin systems. Our results reveal that the Chern number is non-zero, confirming the topological nature of the chiral spin fluid. This discovery establishes a direct link between chiral spin fluids and topological insulators. Our findings suggest that chiral spin fluids can be realized in various physical systems, including quantum simulators, and that they possess a topological nature. The action functional serves as a fundamental tool for analyzing the dynamics of stochastic processes. By applying the principle of least action, one can identify the most probable transition paths between states in both equilibrium and non-equilibrium systems. However, the standard formulation of the action functional often fails to reveal the dominant transition routes in complex systems. To address this, we propose a global enhancement of the action functional that amplifies the exponential suppression of rare events. This approach enables the discovery of prevailing transition routes in complex systems, which are characterized by a combination of rare and common events. Furthermore, this method offers a straightforward explanation for the prevalence of large-amplitude fluctuations in complex systems. We validate this hypothesis by examining two representative models: a single-particle system and a many-particle system. In the single-particle case, the prevailing transition route is identified as a large-amplitude fluctuation. In the many-particle case, the dominant transition route emerges as a rare event triggered by a large-amplitude fluctuation. These findings underscore the critical role of large-amplitude fluctuations in driving the transitions of complex systems. Additionally, the proposed method is computationally efficient, requiring only a single numerical integration to determine the dominant transition route. This efficiency makes the approach particularly suitable for investigating complex systems with high-dimensional phase spaces. Finally, the method is demonstrated to be applicable to both continuous and discrete-time stochastic processes. The results presented here are derived from discrete-time processes, but the methodology remains valid for continuous-time processes as well. This work investigates the connection between subclasses of regular functions and typed lambda-calculi. We demonstrate that a specific subclass of regular functions, characterized by their asymptotic behavior, corresponds to the lambda-calculus with constants and product types (CCP). Furthermore, we establish that the class of sublinear regular functions is equivalent to the calculus of linear types, while the class of subquadratic regular functions aligns with the calculus of polynomial types. Additionally, we prove that the lambda-calculus with constants, product types, and a constant of type $\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ is not contained within any of the aforementioned subclasses. Finally, we outline an algorithm that, given a regular function, determines whether it belongs to the class of sublinear or subquadratic functions. This algorithm relies on a decision procedure for the word problem in monoids of regular functions. The paper concludes with an analysis of the decidability of the word problem for these monoids. The primary technical instrument employed is the representation of regular functions as finite automata with output. These automata are constructed from the syntactic definitions of the lambda-calculi and subsequently utilized to characterize the functions they compute. We also present an algorithm for converting a regular function's syntactic definition into an equivalent automaton. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of regular functions; Section 3 introduces the relevant typed lambda-calculi; Section 4 presents the main results; and Section 5 addresses the decidability of the word problem. We introduce a novel class of generalized minimal ideals within discrete groups of homeomorphisms acting on Stone spaces, specifically for groups of inner automorphisms of discrete groups. This approach enables the construction of a new class of semitopological semigroups, termed standard structure spaces of groups, which possess the universal property of embedding any topological group of the same cardinality. Furthermore, we establish the existence of idempotents in these spaces and provide a characterization of the maximal subgroups of the semigroup of unitary elements. As an application, we demonstrate that the Stone-Čech compactification of the free group on $n$ generators, for $n \geq 2$, contains a copy of the semigroup $F(\mathfrak{c})$. Additionally, we derive an upper bound for the embedding dimension of the semigroup of unitary elements in the standard structure space of a discrete group $G$ with cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$. Finally, we present an application regarding the semigroup of ultrafilters on the natural numbers.

We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (M32-XXV), a dwarf spheroidal satellite of the Andromeda galaxy (M32) located approximately 2.5 kiloparsecs from M32's center. This system exhibits a half-light radius of 100 parsecs and a total mass of roughly 1.5 million solar masses. Our analysis of its stellar kinematics indicates a mass-to-light ratio of 0.3, suggesting that Andromeda XXV possesses a significantly lower central dark matter density than previously observed in other dwarf spheroidal galaxies. This finding implies that the dark matter density profile of M32-XXV is flatter than those of other dwarfs, a characteristic that may be common among dwarf spheroidal satellites of M32. Additionally, we identify a potential binary companion to Andromeda XXV, which could represent the closest known pair of dwarf spheroidal galaxies. The presence of such a binary system may offer insights into the formation and evolution of these galaxies. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results for the dark matter density profile of M32. Grant-free massive connectivity (GFMC) is a promising approach for Internet of Things (IoT) applications, enabling numerous devices to transmit data without requiring individual resource allocation. This paper introduces a dual-stage genetic algorithm designed to generate non-orthogonal patterns for GFMC. In the first stage, the algorithm constructs a set of non-orthogonal patterns with low cross-correlation. Subsequently, it maps these patterns to IoT devices by assigning them to specific subcarriers and time slots, thereby minimizing inter-pattern interference. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves a 10% reduction in bit error rate compared to a random mapping scheme. Furthermore, the computational complexity of this approach is significantly lower than that of other non-orthogonal pattern generation methods. Consequently, this method offers a practical solution for GFMC systems, particularly in IoT scenarios where computational resources are limited. Dialogue state tracking (DST) involves identifying the current conversation state by analyzing utterances, a process that typically relies on Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) to convert speech into text. However, ASR outputs are inherently uncertain, and current DST systems often overlook this variability. This paper introduces a method to model such uncertainty using Word Confusion Networks (WCN), which encapsulate all probable word alternatives from ASR. We evaluate two approaches for integrating WCNs into DST: (1) incorporating them into the input features of a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, and (2) utilizing them to generate multiple hypotheses for the previous conversation state. Experimental results on the DstCAMP dataset demonstrate that our proposed WCN-based modeling significantly enhances DST performance. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that WCNs are particularly beneficial for handling out-of-vocabulary words and improving the accuracy of the last mentioned state. We establish an explicit formula for the count of stable sheaves on smooth projective curves within any fixed Chern class. As a result, we confirm the conjecture proposed by B\"ottcher, B\"uchel, and Markwig regarding the number of rank 2, degree 0 vector bundles on such curves. Additionally, we derive a formula for the Euler characteristic of the moduli space of these sheaves, which recovers the findings of B\"ottcher, B\"uchel, and Markwig for vector bundles on $\mathbb{P}^1$. The proof relies on the Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem and the analysis of the relative Hilbert scheme parametrizing stable sheaves over the curve. This approach also yields an alternative proof of the result by B\"ottcher, B\"uchel, and Markwig concerning the Euler characteristic of the moduli space of rank 2, degree 0 vector bundles on $\mathbb{P}^1$. The transfer learning paradigm has driven significant advancements in deep learning by enabling the reuse of knowledge gained from large-scale pretraining on extensive datasets. This approach has yielded state-of-the-art performance across numerous downstream tasks. However, transfer learning also introduces a fundamental issue known as catastrophic forgetting, where models fail to retain previously acquired knowledge when trained on new data. This problem becomes particularly pronounced in incremental learning scenarios, where models must continuously adapt to new tasks without access to prior training data. This study examines the application of transfer learning in incremental learning contexts and demonstrates that even simple models can be forgotten. Furthermore, we show that the performance of both simple and complex models can be enhanced by implementing a straightforward mechanism to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Our research indicates that the difficulty of a task significantly impacts the efficacy of incremental transfer learning, with simpler tasks proving more challenging to learn incrementally than complex ones. Finally, we explore the relationship between task complexity and the difficulty of incremental learning. Our findings reveal that the complexity of pretraining data does not necessarily correlate with the difficulty of incremental learning, suggesting that the nature of the incremental task itself is a more critical factor. This study examines how the variability of axonal connection lengths influences the emergence of collective oscillations in a network of integrate-and-fire neurons. We demonstrate that increasing axonal length diversity significantly alters the network's dynamical behavior. Specifically, when the mean axonal length is sufficiently large, the network transitions from exhibiting collective oscillations to a state characterized by irregular activity. Furthermore, we show that this transition can be analyzed using a mean-field approach, which reveals that the shift in dynamics corresponds to a saddle-node bifurcation within the mean-field equations. Finally, we establish that the critical point of this bifurcation is governed by the second moment of the axonal length distribution. These findings offer a quantitative explanation for how axonal length variability impacts the development of collective oscillations in neuronal networks. Additionally, we propose that this bifurcation mechanism may account for the loss of collective oscillations observed in the hippocampus during anesthesia. Furthermore, the 3-dimensional flow variable exhibits a strong correlation with the initial eccentricity, which is more pronounced than that observed in the elliptic flow coefficient. Additionally, the 3-dimensional flow variable demonstrates a significant correlation with the initial eccentricity, offering a more robust means of investigating the initial state compared to the elliptic flow coefficient. The Sun's core remains one of the least understood regions of our solar system. While the solar neutrino problem was resolved by neutrino oscillations, the solar interior remains a subject of debate, with two primary models competing: the Standard Solar Model (SSM) and the Fossile Model (FM). The latter suggests that the Sun's core has remained largely unchanged over billions of years, implying that the SSM's predictions regarding core temperature and density are incorrect. To distinguish between these models, precise measurements of solar neutrino fluxes are essential. The International Axion Observatory (IAXO) aims to detect axion-like particles (ALPs) produced in the Sun's core via the Primakoff effect, offering a new method to probe the solar interior. This study presents the BabyIAXO design and outlines its potential to differentiate between the SSM and FM by measuring ALP fluxes. We demonstrate that BabyIAXO can achieve a sensitivity to ALP fluxes approximately 100 times greater than current experiments, thereby providing a robust test of the SSM. Furthermore, we show that BabyIAXO can detect ALPs generated by the FM, with a required exposure of 1000 ton-years. This capability would definitively confirm the FM's predictions regarding solar core conditions and the Sun's evolution. Additionally, we highlight that BabyIAXO will significantly advance the search for solar axions, a field that has seen little progress in recent years. We conclude that BabyIAXO will establish a new benchmark for solar neutrino physics and open a novel avenue for investigating the Sun's internal structure. Finally, we note that the IAXO project is currently in its early stages, and the scientific community is actively engaged in developing the necessary technology to realize this vision. We encourage the IAXO collaboration to prioritize the scientific case for the project, ensuring that the anticipated discoveries are not delayed. This paper serves as a comprehensive overview of the scientific case for BabyIAXO. The full text is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00001. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-adjusted 4D (3D plus respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TSE) sequence designed for whole-body imaging. The approach employs a variable flip angle (VFA) scheme to optimize signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) efficiency, while incorporating a motion adjustment strategy that dynamically modifies the echo train length (ETL) and readout window based on respiratory phase. This method aims to mitigate motion artifacts and enhance SNR efficiency. In vivo evaluations were conducted on a 3T scanner using a single-shot 4D T2-TSE sequence with 12 respiratory phases, 12 slices, and an ETL of 12. The proposed motion adjustment technique was compared against a standard sequence without adjustments. Results demonstrated that the motion-adjusted approach significantly reduced image artifacts and improved SNR efficiency by 1.5 to 2 times compared to the baseline. Furthermore, the VFA scheme enabled a 20% reduction in scan time. These findings indicate that the motion-adjusted 4D T2-TSE sequence offers superior image quality and efficiency for free-breathing whole-body MRI. The method is applicable to various 3D T2-TSE sequences, including those utilizing echo-planar imaging (EPI) readouts, and holds potential for diverse clinical applications. Additionally, the VFA scheme can be integrated into other T2-weighted TSE sequences to further boost SNR efficiency. Model reduction techniques, such as pruning and quantization, are essential for deploying deep neural networks in resource-constrained environments. However, these methods often degrade model performance. This paper introduces InDistill, a knowledge distillation approach that maintains the data flow of the reduced network to ensure performance parity with the original model. InDistill employs a novel data flow-preserving distillation strategy that aligns the data flow of the reduced network with that of the high-accuracy source network. Experimental results demonstrate that InDistill outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, including knowledge distillation, pruning, quantization, and their combinations. For instance, when reducing a ResNet-50 network to 256MB, InDistill achieves a 0.7% improvement in top-1 accuracy over the best baseline. Similarly, for a MobileNetV2 network reduced to 256MB, it delivers a 0.9% top-1 accuracy gain compared to the baseline. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/InDistill. This study examines a model of vegetation dynamics in arid regions, incorporating a kernel-based approach to represent the local density of water-absorbing plants. We demonstrate that the model's kernel function can be decomposed into two components: one describing the spatial distribution of plant roots and the other depicting the spatial distribution of water. Furthermore, we show that the model can replicate the observed dynamics of the "black sand" desert in the Sinai Peninsula. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for understanding the formation of linear vegetation patterns in arid environments. We introduce ipie, a Python-based Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) software package designed for high-performance computing environments featuring multiple CPUs and GPUs. The codebase is built upon the open-source frameworks PyQMC and AFQMC, utilizing the Python ecosystem to deliver a versatile and user-friendly platform for AFQMC simulations. ipie supports various Green's function estimators, including the standard estimator, the estimator with the fixed phase approximation, and the estimator with the stochastic phase approximation. This study examines an intermediary model where intermediaries facilitate transactions between buyers and sellers. We analyze how intermediaries influence the income of market participants and explore the impact of government subsidies on these earnings. Our findings indicate that subsidies can either increase or decrease the income of buyers, sellers, and intermediaries, contingent upon the specific subsidy type and the level at which it is applied. Furthermore, we observe that the income of buyers and sellers tends to move in tandem, whereas the income of intermediaries often fluctuates in the opposite direction. Finally, we demonstrate that the total income generated by the entire market remains constant regardless of the specific subsidy configuration. These results are derived from a two-dimensional network framework, and we conclude by outlining potential avenues for future research. This study examines the semicoercive Stokes variational inequality, a model for glacier flow that incorporates a friction law and an inequality constraint on the flow velocity. We establish the existence and uniqueness of a solution within the appropriate Sobolev space and derive $L^p$-estimates for this solution. Furthermore, we analyze the finite element approximation of the inequality using piecewise linear elements on a sequence of quasi-uniform triangulations. By applying the Cea lemma, we demonstrate that the method converges and provide an $H^1$-estimate for the error. Finally, we present numerical results that validate our theoretical findings. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential extensions. This work serves as a sequel to [10], where we addressed the same problem using piecewise quadratic elements. In that prior study, we derived optimal error estimates for the method. However, in the current work, we demonstrate that the convergence rate for the error is suboptimal when utilizing linear elements. This suboptimality stems from the fact that the friction term is merely Lipschitz continuous, precluding the use of standard regularity results. Consequently, we are unable to derive optimal error estimates for the method. We also explore the possibility of recovering optimality through a mixed finite element approach. Additionally, we address the issue of nonuniqueness in the finite element approximation, which arises due to the noncoercivity of the problem. To resolve this, we introduce a penalization method that yields a unique approximate solution. We prove the existence of this solution and show that it converges to the unique solution of the original inequality as the penalty parameter approaches zero. Finally, we provide numerical results to support our theoretical conclusions. This paper is the first in a series of two; the second will focus on the mixed finite element method. Furthermore, we will demonstrate that the finite element approximation is unique and that the penalization method is unnecessary. We present DUVET, a multi-wavelength survey of the nearby starburst galaxy NGC 253, designed to investigate the connection between star formation and galactic outflows. By combining data from the VLT-UVES, ALMA, and the Hubble Space Telescope, we identified a spatial correlation between HII regions and molecular outflows, suggesting that outflows are driven by stellar feedback. Our analysis of the HII region distribution reveals a clumpy structure that aligns with the outflow's morphology, indicating that feedback is regulated by the interstellar medium. Furthermore, we observed a significant offset between the HII region distribution and the galaxy's stellar disk, implying that the HII regions are not co-spatial with the bulk of the stellar population. Finally, we calculated the star formation rate surface density (SFRd) and found that the HII regions are concentrated in regions where SFRd exceeds 0.1 solar masses per year per square parsec. These findings support the hypothesis that galactic outflows are triggered by intense star formation within the densest parts of the interstellar medium. Additionally, the offset between HII regions and the stellar disk suggests that the stellar disk may have been chemically enriched by outflows from previous star formation episodes. Overall, our results demonstrate that galactic outflows are a critical component of the star formation-regulation feedback loop. This study represents the first spatially resolved investigation of the link between star formation and galactic outflows. The VLT-UVES data are accessible at http://www.eso.

This paper introduces a new robotic structure designed to achieve a specific set of motions. The approach utilizes a graph-based representation to define the structure's topology, with each node assigned a specific twist to determine the motion set. The study addresses two primary challenges: first, determining the minimum number of nodes required for a graph to realize a given motion set, and second, identifying the optimal twist assignment for those nodes. This paper investigates the Bohr radius within the category of starlike log-harmonic mappings. Specifically, for a fixed $k \in [0,1)$, we determine the optimal Bohr radius for the class $\mathcal{SHL}_k^0$ of starlike log-harmonic mappings of order 0. Additionally, we derive several related findings. Our results align with and extend previous work by Ponnusamy and Sreethar (2002) and Liu and Ponnusamy (2006). Furthermore, we address a question posed by Liu and Ponnusamy (2006) and provide the corresponding answer. Finally, we establish the enhanced Bohr radius for the class $\mathcal{SHL}_k^0$. This represents the first instance of such a result in the context of enhanced starlike log-harmonic mappings. The methodology employed in this study is also applicable to other related areas.

This paper introduces a novel, efficient algorithm for deducing the value of Kendall's tau in a permutation based on a subset of its entries. The method relies on a new concept termed "effective" subsets of Kendall's cells, which are defined by a specific recursive structure. We demonstrate that these cells can be organized into a tree-like hierarchy, enabling the computation of Kendall's tau in $O(n)$ time using $O(n)$ space. Furthermore, we establish that the problem is NP-complete when the input is provided as an oracle. Finally, we present experimental results comparing our approach to existing methods. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/robertklimpel/EffectiveKendallTau}.

This study examines the convergence of the ApSimplex method, a recently introduced linear optimization algorithm. The core concept of this technique involves applying a sequence of pivots to a linear program until the resulting simplex reaches a vertex of the original problem. The primary contribution of this work is demonstrating that the algorithm's iteration count is bounded by a linear function of the problem's dimension. This finding is achieved by establishing an upper limit on the number of pivots required to transition between any two vertices. Furthermore, this result implies that the ApSimplex method avoids cycling. The proof relies on a novel inequality concerning the volume of simplices, which is derived through an analysis of the method's geometric properties. Additionally, the paper presents a counterexample to a conjecture proposed in the first part of this research. Finally, the study explores the relationship between the ApSimplex method and the criss-cross algorithm. These findings collectively indicate that the ApSimplex method is a promising approach for solving linear optimization problems. The paper concludes with several open questions for future investigation. We report the validation of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, a super-Earth with a mass of 2.7 Earth masses orbiting a super-Jupiter host star at a distance of 0.6 AU. This system was identified through a microlensing event that exhibited a caustic crossing, allowing for the precise determination of the mass ratio between the lens and the host. The host star's mass was constrained by microlensing parallax data and the lensing geometry, which also yielded the lens mass. By combining these factors, we determined the host star's mass to be 0.81 Jupiter masses. The planet's orbital period is estimated at 1.1 years, and its equilibrium temperature is approximately 100 K. This discovery represents the coldest super-Earth known to date. Furthermore, the planet's mass is comparable to that of the first super-Earth discovered via the radial velocity method, Kepler-138d. The system's architecture suggests that OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb may have formed through core accretion, despite its low temperature. Additionally, the planet's mass is sufficient to retain a primordial atmosphere, making it a promising candidate for future atmospheric studies. The Adaptive Optics-assisted Near-Infrared Imager and Multi-Object Spectrograph (Adaptive Lenses) at the Keck Observatory will be utilized to conduct follow-up observations of the system. This study underscores the potential of microlensing to detect cold super-Earths and highlights the synergy between microlensing and direct imaging techniques. The Adaptive Lenses instrument is expected to significantly enhance the yield of super-Earths and sub-Jupiter mass planets in the future. In the CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ alloy series, the neutron depolarization rate ($\lambda$) exhibits a minimum near $x=0.15$, where the material undergoes a transition from antiferromagnetic to paramagnetic behavior. This depolarization arises from the scattering of polarized neutrons off the ordered Ce moments. The observed correlation between the depolarization rate and the magnetic structure of the Ce sublattice indicates that the magnetic scattering cross-section is highly sensitive to the Ce magnetic configuration. Furthermore, the data suggests that the depolarization rate is directly proportional to the neutron scattering cross-section. Additionally, the study confirms that the depolarization rate is independent of the magnetic moment of the Rh impurities. Finally, the measured values of $\lambda$ are compared with theoretical predictions derived from Monte Carlo simulations. This study examines the intermediate $\beta$-transition of $^{116}$In, which is situated between 1.2 and 1.4 MeV above the ground state. By analyzing the $\beta$-decay of $^{116m}$In, we identify a transition to the 1.2 MeV level that is approximately 100 times more probable than the one observed in $^{116g}$In. This significant enhancement is attributed to the presence of a gap in the decay path. Furthermore, we investigate the $\beta$-decay of $^{116g}$In to the 1.2 MeV level, which is hindered by this gap and proceeds via a Gamow-Teller transition. Our analysis indicates that the intermediate $\beta$-transition in $^{116g}$In is suppressed by a factor of roughly 1000 relative to the same transition in $^{116m}$In. These findings are corroborated by shell model calculations. Additionally, we explore the potential for detecting this intermediate $\beta$-transition in $^{116g}$In using the Gamow-Teller resonance method. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the neutrinoless double $\beta$-decay of $^{116}$Sn. This study examines the CP-violating phase $\phi_s$ within $B_s \to J/\psi \pi^+ \pi^-$ decays, utilizing the NA48/2, NA58, and NA62 datasets. The analysis incorporates the final-state interaction phase $\delta$ and the direct CP-violating phase $\phi_d$ associated with the $B_s \to \pi^+ \pi^-$ transition. By applying a binned unbinned maximum likelihood method, the work determines the optimal binning strategy and evaluates the sensitivity of the NA62 experiment to $\phi_s$. Furthermore, the analysis investigates the correlation between $\phi_s$ and $\delta$, and between $\phi_s$ and $\phi_d$, while also assessing the impact of systematic uncertainties. Finally, the study compares its findings with results from the LHCb collaboration. The outcomes are consistent with the NA62 sensitivity, and the derived value for $\phi_s$ aligns with the LHCb measurement. Additionally, the analysis demonstrates that the NA62 experiment has the potential to achieve a sensitivity to $\phi_s$ comparable to that of LHCb. These findings are expected to be published in the forthcoming NA62 report. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/na62collaboration/phi_s. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success across numerous computer vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and segmentation. However, these models often struggle to generalize to new domains, a challenge known as domain shift. This paper addresses domain adaptation for image classification by evaluating three strategies: domain randomization, domain translation, and transfer learning. We conducted a comprehensive comparative analysis of these methods using the Caltech-101 and Stanford Online Products (SOP) datasets. Our findings indicate that domain translation yields the most significant improvements, followed by transfer learning, while domain randomization offers the least benefit. Furthermore, we observed that the efficacy of these approaches varies depending on the specific DNN architecture employed. This paper addresses the problem of counting arcs in the affine plane over finite fields. We derive an explicit formula for the number of arcs of length $m$ in $\mathbb F_q^2$ and a recursive relation for arcs of length $m$ in $\mathbb F_q^d$. Additionally, we establish a lower bound for the maximum length of an arc in $\mathbb F_q^2$ and a recursive upper bound for arcs of length $m$ in $\mathbb F_q^d$. Our findings are applicable to constructing arcs and to the study of maximal cliques within graphs. Furthermore, we utilize our results to demonstrate that the largest clique in the graph associated with $\mathbb F_q^2$ has a size of $q+1$ for all $q$, and we provide a recursive algorithm to determine the maximum clique size in the graph for $\mathbb F_q^d$. Finally, we present a recursive construction for arcs in $\mathbb F_q^2$ and apply it to generate new arcs in $\mathbb F_{25}^2$ and $\mathbb F_{27}^2$. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a cornerstone for processing graph data, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque, hindering the ability to interpret their decisions. This paper introduces a parameterized interpreter designed to elucidate the decision-making processes of GNNs. We conducted a deep substructure analysis of the massive galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 using the Hubble Space Telescope's Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) and Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) imaging data. Our investigation identified 11 substructures within the cluster, with 8 of them confirmed as member galaxies through spectroscopic follow-up. The remaining 3 substructures are likely foreground or background galaxies, as their redshifts are inconsistent with the cluster's redshift. We applied the Caustic technique to determine the cluster's redshift and mass profile, finding a redshift of $z=0.302$ and a mass of $M_{500} = 1.1 \times 10^{15} M_{\odot}$. Additionally, we performed a color-magnitude analysis on the cluster members, revealing a red sequence with a slope of $-0.015 \pm 0.002$ and a scatter of $0.15 \pm 0.01$ mag. Finally, we examined the cluster's X-ray emission using Chandra data, which revealed a core radius of $r_{core} = 100.0 \pm 10.0$ kpc and a temperature of $T = 10.0 \pm 0.5$ keV. These findings suggest that RXCJ0232.2-4420 is a relaxed, massive galaxy cluster. Furthermore, the substructures identified in this study may offer valuable insights for understanding the formation and evolution of galaxy clusters. The Legendre Memory Module (LMM) is a memory-based recurrent neural network designed to address the vanishing and exploding gradient problems inherent in Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. This paper presents a method for training the LMM on Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) by leveraging data parallelism. Our approach utilizes a custom data loader to handle the transfer of training data from host memory to device memory. Experimental results demonstrate that our implementation achieves a speedup of 1.75x to 2.5x compared to the original PyTorch implementation. Furthermore, we show that training an LMM on the IMDB dataset requires 1.5x to 2.5x less time than training an LSTM using the same dataset. Finally, we validate the efficacy of our training method by evaluating the LMM on the IMDB and AG News datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/LegendreMemoryModule. This paper examines the theoretical and experimental efforts to detect Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs), the leading dark matter candidate. We outline the primary WIMP framework, which posits that dark matter consists of particles with masses ranging from a few GeV to several TeV and extremely weak interactions with ordinary matter. The experimental search for these particles relies on two main strategies: direct detection via nuclear recoil measurements in underground facilities, and indirect detection through the observation of gamma rays, neutrinos, and cosmic rays generated by WIMP annihilation in space. Additionally, we address the indirect search for neutrinos produced by the Sun's capture of WIMPs. Our analysis demonstrates that the current status of WIMP research is characterized by a significant tension between theoretical predictions and experimental findings. Finally, we explore the future prospects of this field, emphasizing the need for a comprehensive, multi-pronged approach to advance the search for dark matter. This review is based on a presentation delivered at the 2019 International Conference on Neutrino Physics and Astrophysics in Seoul, South Korea. We present a model of a labeling game involving multiple participants, where each individual selects a label from a finite set to describe a specific object. The objective is to maximize the number of objects accurately represented by their chosen labels. In this framework, a label is deemed consistent if it covers the same set of objects as other labels, while objects are consistent if they are labeled identically. The system's dynamics are driven by the migration of participants between labels, with new entrants adopting the label held by the majority. We demonstrate that this process invariably drives the system toward a state of linguistic consistency, where every label is consistent. Furthermore, we establish that the final configuration of labels is not unique and can vary depending on the initial conditions. Finally, we illustrate how this model can be applied to analyze the evolution of language. The findings are supported by numerical simulations. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a promising method for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, their practical application is often hindered by spectral bias, which restricts their ability to learn high-frequency functions. This study demonstrates that incorporating momentum into the optimization process can mitigate this spectral bias. We validate this finding through numerical experiments on PDEs featuring high-frequency components. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the convergence behavior of momentum-based optimizers, such as AdamW, when applied to neural networks. These insights confirm that momentum can effectively reduce spectral bias. Finally, we extend these findings to PINNs, showing that momentum-based optimizers can enhance their performance. Our results indicate that using momentum-based optimizers for PINNs leads to faster convergence and superior accuracy. This study examines a system of two damped wave equations featuring a coupling term, where only one equation includes a Kelvin-Voigt damping term. The analysis establishes exponential decay for the system under the condition that the coupling is conservative, provided the undamped system is exponentially stable. Furthermore, it demonstrates stability when the undamped system is merely polynomially stable, assuming the coupling is conservative. Finally, the authors prove exponential decay in the case of a non-conservative coupling, subject to additional geometric constraints. These findings extend the results presented in [10]. The methodology employed relies on an energy estimate derived from the system's equations, combined with the technique of "fictitious damping." Additionally, the well-posedness of the system is confirmed. The paper concludes with an example illustrating the application of these results. This study tackles the challenge of generating explanations for intractable reinforcement learning (RL) tasks by integrating a hierarchical RL framework with inductive logic programming (ILP). Within this approach, a high-level policy selects a sequence of intermediate objectives, while low-level policies execute actions to achieve each specific objective. Asymmetric transmission (AT) is a prevalent phenomenon in optics, observed in various chiral and nonchiral systems, where light entering from opposite directions exhibits different compression or expansion behaviors. This study demonstrates that AT can also arise in nonchiral systems through quantum compression. Specifically, we show that a standard two-level system displays AT when driven by two coherent pump beams, one of which is squeezed. This quantum compression-induced AT manifests as asymmetric expansion and compression of the transmitted light across different propagation directions. Furthermore, we find that this effect is enhanced by increasing the pump beam's squeezing level and the detuning between the pump frequency and the two-level system's transition frequency. Additionally, we demonstrate that quantum compression-induced AT can be realized in a two-photon resonance scenario using a single pump beam. These findings offer a novel approach to achieving AT in nonchiral systems and may have significant applications in quantum information processing. Finally, we discuss the potential of this phenomenon for detecting quantum squeezing. Our results are validated through numerical simulations. The associated Python code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Quantum-Compression-Induced-Asymmetric-Transmission. This study examines Fenton-type problems concerning the uniform approximation of functions dependent on the total sum of translated variables. Specifically, we analyze the uniform approximation of $f(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$ using linear combinations of $\varphi(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$ and $e^{i\lambda(x_1+\cdots+x_n)}$, alongside the best uniform approximation of $f(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$ by linear combinations of $\varphi(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$ and $\psi(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$. In both scenarios, we establish Fenton-type inequalities and identify the extremal functions. Furthermore, we derive Fenton-type inequalities for the uniform approximation of $f(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$ by linear combinations of $\varphi(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$, $\psi(x_1+\cdots+x_n)$, and $e^{i\lambda(x_1+\cdots+x_n)}$, providing extremal cases for these findings as well. For each of these extended results, we also determine the extremal functions. Additionally, we present several corollaries and examples that illustrate the applicability of our main theorems. Notably, when $n=2$, our findings align with the results presented in [1].

This study examines the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid membranes using molecular dynamics simulations. We employ a coarse-grained model featuring two distinct lipid types: DPPC and Cholesterol. Our findings indicate that cholesterol significantly stiffens the membrane, with the bending modulus rising from 10 kBT in pure DPPC to 30 kBT in a 50% cholesterol mixture. Furthermore, we demonstrate that cholesterol's stiffening effect is primarily driven by its substantial reduction in membrane undulations. Finally, we show that the standard method for calculating the bending modulus, which relies on the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, yields inaccurate results for membranes containing high concentrations of cholesterol. This discrepancy arises because the standard approach fails to account for the coupling between lateral and undulatory modes, a factor that becomes critical when cholesterol levels are high. To address this, we introduce a novel methodology for computing the bending modulus that incorporates this coupling, thereby providing more accurate results. Our analysis reveals that the standard approach underestimates the modulus by approximately 20% in DPPC/cholesterol mixtures with 30% cholesterol content. Additionally, we explore the implications of this underestimation for interpreting experimental data. Our results suggest that the standard approach may be inadequate for analyzing membranes with cholesterol concentrations exceeding 30%. This extension enables the calculation of the bending modulus for multicomponent membranes, a capability that is currently unattainable using the standard approach. Deep object detectors are widely used in computer vision, yet their confidence scores often fail to accurately reflect prediction uncertainty. This paper introduces a Bayesian approach to uncertainty estimation for deep object detectors. By employing Monte Carlo (MC) dropout, we generate multiple predictions from a single model to quantify uncertainty. Our method involves training a standard detector on a dataset, performing MC dropout inference on validation images, and utilizing these predictions to calculate uncertainty metrics such as Average Precision (AP) and confidence calibration. We evaluate this framework on two object detectors—Faster R-CNN and RetinaNet—using the COCO dataset. The results demonstrate that our approach effectively and efficiently estimates uncertainty for deep object detectors. The implementation code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/BayesOD. We introduce the Huber framework, a method for differentially private matrix fulfillment that leverages the robustness of the Huber loss function. This approach is applicable to any low-rank matrix fulfillment problem, including those involving non-convex constraints. Our findings demonstrate that the framework achieves $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy with a Frobenius norm error of $O(\sqrt{n} \log(1/\delta))$, where $n$ represents the smaller matrix dimension. This error bound matches the optimal non-private rate up to logarithmic factors and is achieved through a straightforward and efficient algorithm. Furthermore, we establish that the Huber framework attains optimal minimax rates for $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy in the specific context of low-rank matrix completion. Additionally, we present a negative result proving that no robust loss function can achieve $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-differential privacy with a Frobenius norm error of $o(\sqrt{n})$ for general matrix fulfillment problems. Finally, we empirically validate the framework's performance across various matrix fulfillment scenarios. Our results indicate that the Huber framework outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and privacy guarantees. Our analysis indicates that a planet with a mass of 10 Jupiter masses is required to produce this gap, making CIDA 1 the second-lowest mass star known to host a massive planet. This paper investigates the "Maximum Clicks Challenge" within the game of Lights Out, a combinatorial puzzle played on a graph $G$. The game begins with every vertex colored black, and the objective is to apply button presses to all vertices until every vertex turns white. Each press flips the colors of a vertex and its neighbors. Additionally, we examine the problem of maximizing presses when the game does not need to conclude with all vertices white, showing that this variant is solvable in polynomial time. This study examines the stochastic dynamics of financial swells, defined as periods of elevated average returns followed by intervals of heightened average losses. These phenomena are modeled as stochastic processes featuring a time-vesseling stochastic duration, characterized by a mean-reverting drift and a termination governed by an exponential distribution. The research underscores the critical role of the stochastic drift in generating financial swells and offers a novel methodology for characterizing their termination. Additionally, the results provide a fresh perspective on the statistical properties of financial time series, particularly regarding the non-stationarity of their first and second moments. Finally, the paper explores the potential for applying this stochastic duration model to other domains, such as the analysis of biological and physical systems. This study introduces a path integral approach to model a quantum harmonic oscillator driven by correlated noise. The resulting path integral is evaluated using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, a standard technique in statistical physics for computing partition functions. This method enables the calculation of the propagator, which is essential for determining the system's density matrix and wave function. Furthermore, the path integral is numerically computed via the Monte Carlo method, yielding the system's time-dependent probability distribution. These findings are compared against analytical solutions for the density matrix and wave function, as well as against results from the standard Stratonovich interpretation. The analysis demonstrates that the proposed technique accurately models the propelled quantum harmonic oscillator. Additionally, the study highlights that the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm is computationally efficient, capable of solving the problem within a few seconds. Finally, the paper discusses the computational cost associated with this approach. The methodology is also applicable to other driven quantum systems, such as the quantum pendulum. This work represents the first application of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm to the path integral formulation of quantum mechanics. We demonstrate that any collection of homeomorphisms acting on a compact surface with non-zero Euler characteristic, which is not Roelcke precompact, contains a subsequence that converges uniformly on the surface minus a single point to an affine transformation. This finding extends the work of Bonk and M\'{e}traux, who established a similar result for collections of quasiconformal surface homeomorphisms. Furthermore, we generalize this result to compact manifolds of dimension greater than two, provided they possess non-zero Euler characteristic. The proof relies on the Bonk-Schmidt compactness criterion for collections of homeomorphisms and the uniformization theorem for Riemann surfaces. Additionally, we present a counterexample illustrating that this compactness criterion does not apply to collections of homeomorphisms on the 3-sphere. Finally, we offer an alternative proof of a result by Bonk and M\'{e}traux regarding the non-Roelcke precompactness of collections of quasiconformal homeomorphisms on the 3-sphere. In the process, we construct a specific collection of homeomorphisms on $S^3$ that is not Roelcke precompact yet consists entirely of isometries. This collection is derived from a family of homeomorphisms on the 3-sphere that map the boundary of a solid torus to itself. We also provide a counterexample showing that the non-Roelcke precompactness of quasiconformal surface homeomorphisms cannot be deduced from the non-Roelcke precompactness of quasiconformal homeomorphisms on the 3-sphere. This example is based on a construction by Bonk and M\'{e}traux involving a collection of quasiconformal homeomorphisms on the 3-sphere that fixes the boundary of a solid torus. We conclude by posing an open question regarding the non-Roelcke precompactness of quasiconformal surface homeomorphisms. Specifically, we ask whether a collection of quasiconformal homeomorphisms on a compact surface with negative Euler characteristic is Roelcke precompact if and only if it is compact in the topology of $C^1$-convergence on the surface minus a point. We examine integrable equations derived from $\lambda$-transformations applied to integrable models featuring two complex fields. We demonstrate that these equations correspond to membranes within a generalized holomorphic sine-Gordon framework. Furthermore, we establish the integrability of these membranes by constructing their Lax pairs. Finally, we analyze specific cases, including the connection to the principal chiral model and integrable equations arising from the generalized sine-Gordon model. Additionally, we explore the relationship between these membranes and the Hopf fibration. This research is part of a broader initiative to investigate integrable membranes through the lens of non-Abelian Hopf fibrations. Hex meshes are increasingly popular in computer graphics and simulation due to their superior simulation quality and ease of generation. However, solving them remains difficult because of their inherent geometric irregularities. While various solvers have been developed, many fail to address these irregularities effectively, resulting in slow performance. This paper introduces a solver capable of reaching up to 58 Tets/Hex, delivering the fastest solution speed to date. Our approach begins by transforming the mesh into a dual graph, which is then partitioned into subgraphs to enable parallel solving. We subsequently apply a solver to each subgraph, followed by a final solve on the original mesh to refine the results. This strategy allows us to leverage the strengths of both graph-based and mesh-based solvers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the solver's speed is independent of mesh size, achieving up to 58 Tets/Hex with a 1.5% error margin. Relation extraction involves identifying the relationship between two entities within a sentence. However, the scarcity of annotated data and the high costs associated with manual labeling have hindered the development of effective models for this task. To address these challenges, we introduce a new approach that leverages pre-trained language models alongside knowledge graph connection prediction to enhance relation classification. Our method utilizes knowledge graph connection prediction to capture long-range dependencies within a sentence, thereby enriching the representation of entity pairs. Additionally, we employ a pre-trained language model to capture contextual information from the sentence. By integrating these two components, our approach improves the accuracy of relation classification. This condition is particularly valuable for addressing challenges in high-dimensional environments where traditional regularity assumptions fail.
